explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but watch the little word Peter, the apostle writing this letter, uses. He says, “Rid yourselves, therefore, of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander.” That word is “all,” not “most.” I once tried to clean up only most of the crumbs on my counter, and I'm telling you, the leftovers always find you.

That's right, and it all comes down to one little word. Peter, the apostle writing this letter, says to rid yourselves “…of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander.” Not most of them, and not just the ones that are easy to give up. Every last crumb goes.

Milk it is! Peter says, “Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk…” A newborn doesn't need to be talked into wanting it, and that's the picture Peter picks. The milk has a purpose too: “…so that by it you may grow up in your salvation…”

Nice guess, but Peter doesn't bring bread into this one. He says, “Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk…” Milk is what a newborn cries for, which is why the picture works so well. Bread would've been a whole different kind of baby.

Water makes sense as a pick, but it's not what Peter says. He says, “Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk…” Think of what a hungry newborn is hollering for, and you'll see why he chose it. Milk is the one.

explanations.answer: So they can grow up in their salvation
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Peter says to crave the milk “…so that by it you may grow up in your salvation…” Newborns don't stay newborns, and that's the whole idea. The growing comes by the milk.

explanations.answer: So they can teach others right away
explanations.explanation: That sounds good, but Peter doesn't say that here. He says to crave the milk “…so that by it you may grow up in your salvation…” The goal he names is growing up. Nobody hands a newborn a microphone, friend.

explanations.answer: So they never need help again
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't promise that, friend. He says to crave the milk “…so that by it you may grow up in your salvation…” The goal he gives is growing, and he says nothing about never needing help. Honestly, I'm still asking for help, and I've got ovens.
True! Peter says to crave the milk “…now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.” He's talking to people who have already had a taste. That's why the craving makes sense.
This one's true, friend. Peter says to crave the milk “…now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.” The taste has already happened for these believers. Peter is building on it.

Chosen and precious, that's the one. Peter says the living stone is “…rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight…” Men rejected Him, but in God's sight He is chosen and precious. I know a little about being shoved to the back of a junk drawer and then called out of it, and it's a very good feeling.

Hidden and waiting sounds like a mystery novel, but it's not what Peter says. He says the living stone is “…rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight…” Men rejected the stone, and in God's sight it is chosen and precious.

That's how the rejecters saw it, maybe, but Peter doesn't say that. He says the living stone is “…rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight…” Chosen and precious is nothing like plain and ordinary. In God's sight, this stone stands out.

A spiritual house, you got it! Peter says the believers, “…like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house…” In Peter's picture, believers aren't stones sitting in a pile. They're being built into a building.

A wall is made of stones, so I see the thinking. But Peter says the believers, “…like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house…” A house, not a city wall. A house is where you live, and a wall is mostly for standing around.

A watchtower is stones piled up high, but that's not what Peter has in mind. He says the believers, “…like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house…” It's a house, friend. Nobody's up there with binoculars.

Priesthood! Peter says the living stones are being built “…to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.” The house comes with a job attached. The job is offering spiritual sacrifices to God.

Family is a warm guess, but it's not the word in this verse. Peter says the living stones are being built “…to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices…” A priesthood is the group that offers the sacrifices. Peter gives the house a job, not just a place to gather.

A choir would be a nice sound, but Peter doesn't say choir here. He says the living stones are being built “…to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices…” It's a priesthood, and that's the group doing the offering.
Jesus Christ, that's it. Peter says the sacrifices are “…acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.” The offering doesn't get its welcome from how fancy it is. It comes through Him.

Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, so I get it. But Peter says the sacrifices are “…acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.” The person in this verse is Jesus. He's the one Peter names.

Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), is a big name, I'll give you that. But Peter says the sacrifices are “…acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.” Peter names Jesus here, and nobody else. Keep that name close, friend.

explanations.answer: They will never be put to shame
explanations.explanation: They will never be put to shame, you got it! The Scripture says, “…the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” That's a promise worth putting on the fridge. Shame doesn't get the last word.

That would be nice, but it's not what the Scripture says. It says, “…the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” Never put to shame is the promise. Peter doesn't say anything about trouble in this verse.
That would be quite a promise, but the Scripture doesn't say it. It says, “…the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” Shame is the thing that's promised away.
Peter splits it in two, so keep reading. He says, “To you who believe, then, this stone is precious.” Then he turns to “…those who do not believe…” The precious part is for the believers.
False is right. Peter says, “To you who believe, then, this stone is precious.” Then he turns to those who do not believe and speaks about them separately. So precious is how the believers see it.

Because they disobey the word, that's the reason Peter gives. He says, “They stumble because they disobey the word…” The reason is right there in the verse, so no guessing needed. Good reading, baker.

explanations.answer: Because no one ever warned them
explanations.explanation: Ooh, that one sounds fair, but it's not Peter's reason, friend. He says, “They stumble because they disobey the word…” The reason is sitting right there in the verse, no detective work needed. Warnings never come up at all.

explanations.answer: Because the stone is hidden from them
explanations.explanation: Hidden would be one reason, but it's not Peter's. He says, “They stumble because they disobey the word…” The stone isn't described as hidden, so there's no hide and seek here. The reason he gives is disobeying the word.

explanations.answer: A people for God's own possession
explanations.explanation: A people for God's own possession, you got it. Peter says, “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession…” Look at that list. Every title is one more way of saying the believers belong to Him.

explanations.answer: A people of great wealth and power
explanations.explanation: That sounds grand, but wealth and power aren't in Peter's list. He says, “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession…” The last title is about who they belong to, not what they own.

explanations.answer: A people scattered without a home
explanations.explanation: That's not one of the names in this verse. Peter says, “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession…” Every title in the list says they belong to God. Nothing in it says they belong nowhere.

explanations.answer: To proclaim the virtues of the One who called them
explanations.explanation: Proclaim it is! Peter says they are “…to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.” The names come first, and then comes the job. You get to tell people what He's like.

explanations.answer: To rule over every nation on the earth
explanations.explanation: Royal priesthood might make that sound right, but Peter doesn't say it. He says they are “…to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.” The job is proclaiming, and ruling isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: To keep to themselves and stay safe from harm
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Peter says. He says they are “…to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.” You can't proclaim anything while keeping to yourself. Keeping quiet isn't in the verse.

Light is the word. Peter says God “…called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.” I understand that move from dark to bright, because an angel once called me out of a dusty junk drawer where I had sat for years.
Rest is a lovely word, but it's not what's in this verse. Peter says God “…called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.” Darkness and light are a matched pair. Rest has no seat at this table.

Kingdom does sound big enough to fit, but that's not Peter's word here. He says God “…called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.” Darkness is where they were called from, and light is where they were called to.
True! Peter says, “Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God…” That's a before and an after in one sentence. Peter puts the "once" and the "now" side by side.
This one is true. Peter says, “Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God…” The before and the after are both right there. Now they belong to God.

Mercy, that's the one. Peter says, “once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.” That's a before and after worth sticking on the cookie box. Once it hadn't been received, and now it has.
Riches would be nice, but Peter doesn't say that. He says, “once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.” The thing they now have is mercy. Nothing about money in that verse.

Strength is a good thing to want, but that's not the word. Peter says, “once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.” I'd sign up for extra strength on a long bake day, but this before and after names just one thing.
